content: 1. Technical Support for Business Operations Amid Climate Change: As climate change increasingly impacts the availability and quality of source water, Teuk Saat 1001 has been actively developing strategies to enhance preparedness and response. These include connecting water kiosks to alternative water sources, coordinating logistics between treatment plants in varying conditions, assessing vulnerabilities in water sources, and expanding laboratory testing to detect emerging climate-related contaminants. 2. Risk-Based Surveillance in Nigeria: The 2023 Nigerian Guidelines for Rural Drinking Water Quality Monitoring emphasize a risk-based approach to surveillance. High-risk sites are prioritized for more frequent inspections. Local government authorities are required to conduct sanitary inspections and water quality testing every six months during both rainy and dry seasons. These inspections cover water sources, transport containers, storage facilities, and user practices. Additionally, inspections are conducted during waterborne disease outbreaks or when contamination is detected through community monitoring. Community members are trained to test water sources monthly for microbial safety using cost-effective presence-absence testing methods, such as hydrogen sulfide vials, which help identify high-priority sites for further surveillance. 3. Risk-Based Surveillance in South Australia: In South Australia, the Safe Drinking Water Act 2011 mandates risk management plans for water supplies, which are audited annually or biennially based on risk levels. High-risk water supplies, such as those serving vulnerable populations in childcare or healthcare facilities, are inspected more frequently and by highly qualified practitioners. 4. Optimizing Surveillance Resources in England: In England, local authorities regulate approximately 35,000 private water supplies, primarily in rural areas. Due to resource limitations, only 38% of required risk assessments were up-to-date in 2022, and water quality testing was often below the required frequency. To maximize public health benefits, authorities prioritize high-risk supplies, such as those serving larger populations or commercial activities, for site visits and risk assessments. 5. Training and Knowledge Exchange in India: Under the Jal Jeevan Mission, launched in 2019, the Indian government aims to provide functional household tap connections to every rural household by 2024. This program integrates water quality monitoring by certified laboratories with community-led testing, often conducted by women using simple water testing kits. Over 10 million water samples have been tested as of 2023. To address gaps in water quality management, a one-month online training course was developed, training 1,600 water quality champions. A knowledge exchange forum and a Digital Academy have also been established to scale these efforts nationwide. 6. Digitized Sanitary Inspections in Iceland: Iceland has developed digitized sanitary inspection (SI) forms to support health inspectors in monitoring water supplies, particularly in rural areas. These forms cover 10 dimensions, including construction, maintenance, pollution risks, and service levels. Inspections are conducted using iPads, enabling standardized data collection and automated risk scoring. This approach has improved data quality, reduced variability, and professionalized health inspection functions. 7. Sustainable Financing for Water Regulation in Zambia: Zambia’s National Water Supply and Sanitation Council, established in 2000, oversees regulatory functions, including water quality monitoring. A sustainable financing mechanism, primarily funded by a 2% levy on commercial utilities’ revenues, covers 90% of operational costs. Government grants and development partner resources are used for specific activities, such as strategy development. 8. Joint Risk Assessment in Serbia: In Serbia, a nationwide survey in 2016 assessed sanitary inspection scores and E. coli test results from over 1,300 rural water supplies. Approximately one-third of samples failed microbial standards, and 30-40% of supplies required urgent improvement. Findings highlighted the need for proactive risk management and supported the case for mandatory water safety plans. 9. Collaborative Surveillance in Indonesia: In Indonesia, environmental health workers conduct sanitary inspections (SIs) tailored to various water supply technologies. Results are entered into an electronic system, and detailed reports are prepared for stakeholders. Beginning in 2024, SIs will be complemented by water safety plan audits. 10. Corrective Action Monitoring in the Occupied Palestinian Territory: The Ministry of Health in the occupied Palestinian territory oversees water quality surveillance, testing for parameters such as chlorine, E. coli, nitrates, and heavy metals. When issues are identified, stakeholders collaborate to determine root causes and implement corrective actions. 11. Improved Data Management in Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone has faced challenges in using water supply data for decision-making due to unclear institutional frameworks and limited technical capacity. In 2019, the Ministry of Water Resources launched a National Digital Monitoring Approach, requiring data sharing on a global repository. Over 300 staff have been trained in data management, and efforts are underway to integrate routine monitoring into district water and sanitation plans. 12. Tracking WASH Financing in Mali: Mali has developed WASH accounts to monitor sector spending and address financing gaps. Initial findings revealed that only 53% of funding needs were met, with significant disparities between rural and urban areas. Subsequent cycles expanded data collection to include hygiene and WASH in schools and health centers. Findings have informed funding dialogues, leading to increased government and donor contributions, as well as tariff reforms to generate additional revenue while ensuring equitable service delivery. These detailed insights reflect the diverse approaches and challenges in water quality monitoring, surveillance, and management across different regions.
